name: Micro-cracked
describes: White finishes after drying and years of movement: lime shrinks slightly as it dries and crazes if the finish dried too fast; gypsum expands slightly as it sets, so a cast or fibrous length cracks from drying stress, movement at joints and fixings, or a corroding armature rather than from shrinkage; coatings on casts and thick limewash craze on their own. Hairline cracks open and close with the seasons.

crazing.state: A fine web of cracks in a lime finishing coat that dried too quickly; controlled at making by re-wetting, scouring and polishing.
crazing.source: Napier, W. & Jenkins, M. (2018) Inform Guide: Plain Lime Plastering. Historic Environment Scotland, https://www.historicenvironment.scot/archives-and-research/publications/publication/?publicationId=67d4d72c-7b8c-4622-a244-a94b01090177

shrinkage.state: Lime shrinks slightly as it dries; shrinkage cracks are likely as a lime coat dries and are pressed back and re-worked; plaster laid thin cracks and soon decays.
shrinkage.source: Ratcliffe, T. (1997) The Use of Gypsum Plaster, https://www.buildingconservation.com/articles/gypsum/gypsum_plaster.htm; Ratcliffe, T. (2006) Internal Lime-Plastering, https://www.buildingconservation.com/articles/internallimeplast/lime_plaster.htm; Vitruvius, De Architectura VII.3.9, trans. J. Gwilt (1826), https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Vitruvius/7*.html

gypsumExpansion.note: gypsum grows as it sets, so casts and fibrous lengths do not shrink-craze; their cracks come from drying stress, movement and fixings
gypsumExpansion.source: USG IG1937-USA-ENG rev. 1-20 (No. 1 Moulding Plaster), https://www.usg.com/content/dam/USG_Marketing_Communications/united_states/product_promotional_materials/finished_assets/usg-no-1-moulding-plaster-submital-southard-IG1937.pdf; USG IG1375-USA-ENG rev. 8-24 (No. 1 Casting Plaster), https://www.usg.com/content/dam/USG/pdpmovedocuments/usg-no-1-casting-plaster-data-en-IG1375.pdf

castDrying.state: Casts may crack if dried too quickly.
castDrying.source: Brigham, W.T. (1874), pp. 27-29, as quoted in Payne, E.M. (2020) The Conservation of Plaster Casts in the Nineteenth Century. Studies in Conservation 65(1), 37-58, https://doi.org/10.1080/00393630.2019.1610845

armature.state: Humidity is taken through the plaster to the iron armatures inside casts, which corrode.
armature.source: Healey-Dilkes, S. & Sonntag, M. (2020) Preserving Monumental Plaster Casts in a Historic Building: A Conservation Approach at the Victoria & Albert Museum London. Objects Specialty Group Postprints 27, 75-111, https://resources.culturalheritage.org/osg-postprints/v27/healey-dilkes/

coatings.state: On a cast that had been painted and waxed, the old paint cracks, peels and flakes; hairline cracks, dents and historic repairs accompany it.
coatings.source: Puisto, J. (2014) David revealed. V&A Blog, https://www.vam.ac.uk/blog/caring-for-our-collections/david-revealed

limewashCraze.source: Bennett, B. (1997) Awash with Colour: The Decorative and Protective Roles of Limewash. The Building Conservation Directory, https://www.buildingconservation.com/articles/decorative-protective-limewash/decorative-protective-limewash.htm

structural.state: Cracks from structural movement, loading and differential movement between dissimilar materials follow the structure and joints below; on lath, unstaggered lath joints make cracks, so joints are staggered at 600-900 mm.

seasonal.state: Hairline cracks can open and close through the seasons with moisture and temperature; they usually need no repair.

fibrousFixings.state: Fibrous plaster ties (wads) weaken as the hessian inside decays, over a service life of about 80 years, while looking sound from outside; ceilings sag, crack and can fall.

hessianServiceLife.source: Clifford, R. (2016) Maintaining Large Fibrous Plaster Ceilings. The Building Conservation Directory, https://www.buildingconservation.com/articles/fibrous-plaster-ceilings/fibrous-plaster-ceilings.htm; Harrison, D. (1999), https://www.buildingconservation.com/articles/theatre/theatre.htm

hairline.asReported: Category 0: hairline cracks less than 0.1 mm; no repair needed
hairline.source: BRE Digest 251 (revised 1995) Assessment of damage in low-rise buildings, categories as given at https://www.designingbuildings.co.uk/wiki/Cracking%20and%20building%20movement

fine.asReported: Category 1: fine cracks up to 1 mm, generally restricted to internal wall finishes, treated by normal decoration

easilyFilled.asReported: Category 2: up to 5 mm, easily filled

bySubstance.lime-plaster: Crazing (a closed polygonal web) on patches of finish that dried fast; single hairlines following the masonry or the coffer ribs below. Widths within categories 0-1.
bySubstance.fibrous-plaster: Straight hairlines along joints between cast lengths and at fixings; no shrinkage craze.
bySubstance.plaster-of-paris: Few, discrete cracks: across slender parts and at old joins; cracked, peeling paint or shellac coats; corroding armatures inside.
bySubstance.limewash: A fine craze where coats were thick.

drivers.driver: joints between pieces and substrate joints
arris proximity (cracks and chips start at edges)

drivers.owner: a making-time decision recorded on the piece; not in FMatterPieceLayout (see unverified)

unverified.field: terms.crazing (cell size of a craze web)
unverified.reason: No measured cell size for lime crazing was found.
Rust staining and cracking along a corroding armature are the expected trace, but the sources read only name the corrosion.
Cracks commonly read darker because dirt collects in them, but no source was found that measures it; the soiling history would carry it.
FMatterPieceLayout has no slot for a making-time drying condition; the spare vertex channel or the piece table would need one. Reported as a gap, not worked around.

Clifford, R. (2016); Harrison, D. (1999). The Building Conservation Directory.
Healey-Dilkes, S. & Sonntag, M. (2020) Objects Specialty Group Postprints 27, 75-111.
Napier, W. & Jenkins, M. (2018) Inform Guide: Plain Lime Plastering. Historic Environment Scotland.
Payne, E.M. (2020) Studies in Conservation 65(1), 37-58 (quoting Brigham 1874).
Puisto, J. (2014) David revealed. V&A Blog.
